title: Jacobians and generalized Jacobians
summary: The library develops both Jacobians and Generalized Jacobians: it constructs full moduli over arbitrary fields and proves the associated existence and unique factorization results for maps from open curves to commutative algebraic groups. Further results relate curves to étale cohomology and Tate modules.
overview: A Jacobian gives a curve's degree-zero divisor theory the structure of an algebraic group. The library constructs it over the original field, without requiring a rational point for the construction. A chosen rational point gives an Abel–Jacobi map through which every pointed map to an abelian variety factors uniquely.

Generalized Jacobians extend this factorization theory to open curves and targets that need not be proper. For a map to a separated commutative group scheme locally of finite type, the library constructs a full Cartier modulus over the original field and proves unique equivariant factorization through the intrinsic Picard-one scheme for that modulus. The original open domain is preserved, and no rational curve point or perfectness assumption is required. Choosing a rational point sent to the identity gives the corresponding unique group homomorphism from the generalized Jacobian. Over an algebraically closed field, an actual regular map also has a least full conductor; the conductor of a map into a product is the coefficientwise maximum of those of its components.

Over algebraically closed fields of characteristic zero, the selected cohomology results measure genus and the contribution of punctures. The Tate comparison assumes a representing Picard object and compatibility with divisor classes; the Weil-pairing result proves nondegeneracy for supplied divisorial pairing data. Independent Lie, Witt, symmetric-product and analytic comparison results are outside this selection.
scopeNote: The generalized-Jacobian factorization is over arbitrary fields and constructs its modulus from the original map; uniqueness concerns the factor pair for the returned modulus. The Tate comparison takes a representing Picard object and explicit Abel–Jacobi class compatibility as input. The Weil-pairing entry proves nondegeneracy for supplied divisorial pairing data. The selection does not assert the independent Lie, Witt or analytic comparison theorems.

entries.title: Pointed maps from curves to abelian varieties factor uniquely through Abel–Jacobi
entries.summary: Every pointed morphism from the curve to an abelian variety factors uniquely through the fixed Jacobian.
statement: Let $k$ be a field, let $C/k$ be smooth, proper, geometrically irreducible, and of relative dimension $1$, and choose $P\in C(k)$. Let $A/k$ be a smooth proper geometrically irreducible group scheme. For a $k$-morphism $f:C\to A$ with $f(P)=0$,
$$\exists!\,g:J_C\longrightarrow A\quad\text{such that}\quad f=g\circ a_P.$$
The quantified $g$ in the cited declaration is a morphism in the category of schemes over $k$.
discussion: This universal property reduces the study of pointed maps from the curve to the study of maps out of its Jacobian. Sending the base point to zero removes translation freedom, and uniqueness makes the factorization a characterization of the Jacobian. It is the curve case of the Albanese viewpoint, which characterizes a variety through its maps to abelian varieties; Milne develops it in Section 6.
history: The Albanese viewpoint characterizes a variety by its maps to abelian varieties. For a pointed curve, its Jacobian has this universal role. Milne treats this characterization in Section 6, alongside the duality theory of Jacobians.

entries.title: Generalized Jacobians: existence of a modulus and unique factorization
entries.summary: Every map from a nonempty open curve to a separated commutative group locally of finite type constructs a full modulus and a unique equivariant Picard-one factorization over its original field.
statement: Let $k$ be any field, let $C/k$ be a smooth proper geometrically integral curve, let $U\subseteq C$ be a nonempty open subscheme, and let $G/k$ be a separated commutative group scheme locally of finite type. Given a $k$-morphism $q:U\to G$, there is a full effective Cartier divisor $D$ over $k$ with $C\setminus|D|=U$ for which $q$ satisfies the geometric modulus condition.

For this returned divisor, let $J_D$ be the generalized Jacobian, $J_D^1$ its intrinsic Picard-one torsor, and $a_D^1:U\to J_D^1$ the Abel map. There is a unique pair consisting of a group-scheme morphism $\phi:J_D\to G$ and a $k$-morphism $F:J_D^1\to G$ such that
$$q=F\circ a_D^1,\qquad F(a\cdot x)=\phi(a)F(x)$$

where equivariance holds on points valued in every $k$-scheme. Neither a rational point of $C$, a preassigned modulus, nor perfectness of $k$ is required. The target need not be smooth or connected. Uniqueness is for the pair $(\phi,F)$ with the returned $D$ fixed, not for the divisor itself.

If a point $\varepsilon\in U(k)$ is supplied and $q(\varepsilon)=1$, there is also a direct pointed form: the map constructs such a divisor $D$ and a unique group-scheme morphism $\phi:J_D\to G$ with $q=\phi\circ a_{D,\varepsilon}$. Two maps from the same $U$ can be given a common ground-field modulus.
discussion: A modulus retains the multiplicities of the boundary, so it can control maps to groups beyond the proper targets handled by the ordinary Jacobian. This theorem starts with the actual map, constructs the needed divisor without shrinking its domain, and supplies the algebraic factorization. The Picard-one torsor records the absence of a chosen origin: selecting a rational base point is unnecessary.

Serre develops maps from curves to commutative groups and generalized Jacobians in Chapters III and V of Algebraic Groups and Class Fields. The formal result links modulus existence to the constructed group and torsor over the original field, while keeping the full Cartier divisor and the equivariance equation.
history: The modulus approach connects the mapping properties of open curves with generalized Jacobians. Chapters III and V of Serre's Algebraic Groups and Class Fields provide the mathematical reference for these two parts.

entries.title: Least conductors exist, and the conductor of a product map is their coefficientwise maximum
entries.summary: An actual map from an open curve constructs its unique least full conductor, with an exact coefficientwise formula for product-valued maps.
statement: Let $k$ be algebraically closed in any characteristic, let $C/k$ be a smooth proper integral curve, let $U\subseteq C$ be nonempty, and let $q:U\to G$ be a morphism to a separated commutative group scheme locally of finite type. Let $a_q$ be its function on places with values in $G(k)$, equal to the actual point values on $U$ and extended by the identity outside $U$. There is a unique effective place modulus $D_q$ such that, for every effective place modulus $E$,
$$a_q\text{ has full modulus }E\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad D_q\le E.$$

In additive notation, having full modulus $E$ means $\sum_v\operatorname{ord}_v(f)a_q(v)=0$ for every nonzero rational function $f\equiv1\pmod E$. Thus the conductor here classifies moduli of the specified point-value function on all places.

The inequality compares every place multiplicity. The conductor has coefficient zero at all places centered in $U$; its support may be strictly smaller than $C\setminus U$. The actual map supplies both a modulus and its unique reciprocal local symbol, without requiring either as input.
For another such map $r:U\to H$, the conductor of the map into the product group satisfies
$$D_{(q,r)}=D_q\vee D_r,\qquad D_{(q,r)}(v)=\max\{D_q(v),D_r(v)\}.$$
discussion: A modulus can often be enlarged, so existence alone leaves many choices. The conductor removes that ambiguity by specifying the least allowed multiplicity at every place. Classifying all moduli as those above it is stronger than finding a modulus of minimum total degree.

For a map to a product group, each coordinate imposes its own condition and the least simultaneous bound is their coefficientwise maximum. The calculation uses the actual regular maps and applies to nonproper targets as well. The local-symbol and modulus viewpoint is developed in Serre’s Algebraic Groups and Class Fields.
history: Serre’s treatment of maps from curves to commutative algebraic groups uses moduli and local symbols to describe their boundary behavior and their relation to generalized Jacobians.

entries.title: A pointed genus-one curve is isomorphic to its Jacobian
entries.summary: In characteristic zero, the constructed Abel–Jacobi map for a genus-one curve is an isomorphism.
statement: Let $K$ be algebraically closed of characteristic $0$, let $C$ be the smooth proper curve model of a one-variable function field $F/K$, and choose $P\in C(K)$. If $g(F/K)=1$, the theorem constructs a representing degree-zero Picard object $J$, together with
$$a_P:C\xrightarrow{\sim}J,\qquad a_P(P)=0.$$
The conclusion includes smoothness, properness, geometric connectedness, and the required Picard representation data for $J$.
discussion: The chosen point becomes the identity, and the curve acquires the group structure familiar from elliptic curves. Thus a base point supplies the origin needed to identify a genus-one curve with a group. This connection belongs to classical Jacobian theory: Milne's treatment of canonical maps explains it through degree-zero divisor classes, while his Abelian Varieties describes the role of the identity in the group structure.
history: The connection between genus-one curves and elliptic curves is part of the classical Jacobian theory. Milne's treatment of canonical maps explains the degree-zero divisor-class description; his Abelian Varieties also shows how the identity point governs the group structure on an abelian variety.

entries.title: Cardinality of étale H¹ of a proper curve: the genus formula
entries.summary: The actual first étale cohomology group with roots-of-unity coefficients has the expected genus-dependent cardinality.
statement: Let $K$ be algebraically closed of characteristic $0$, and let $C$ be a geometrically integral smooth proper curve model of $F/K$, equipped with a $K$-point and a geometric point. For $n\ge1$,
$$\#H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C,\underline{\mu_n(K)})=n^{2g(F/K)}.$$
The coefficient object is the constant étale sheaf on the finite abelian group $\mu_n(K)$.
discussion: Kummer theory connects first étale cohomology with torsion line bundles, and the Jacobian realizes that torsion geometrically. The count $n^{2g}$ therefore links the genus to the size of the curve's finite abelian covering data. SGA 1 established the fundamental-group language for these covers; Milne's Jacobian Varieties, Section 9, develops their relation with the torsion of the Jacobian.
history: SGA 1 established the fundamental-group language for finite étale covers. In the Jacobian setting, the relation between abelian covers and torsion is developed in Milne's Jacobian Varieties, Section 9; Kummer theory provides the cohomological expression used here.

entries.title: Cardinality of étale H¹ of an open curve: the genus and boundary formula
entries.summary: For a nonempty finite boundary, the first étale cohomology count gains r−1 boundary directions.
statement: Let $K$ be algebraically closed of characteristic $0$, and let $C$ be a smooth proper curve model of genus $g$ with a $K$-point. Let $j:U\hookrightarrow C$ be a dense open immersion with $U$ integral and quasi-compact. Suppose the boundary has $r\ge1$ places, and choose a geometric point of $U$. Then, for $n\ge1$,
$$\#H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\underline{\mu_n(K)})=n^{\,2g+r-1}.$$
discussion: Each puncture contributes boundary information, while the degree relation ties those contributions together. The exponent $2g+r-1$ separates the roles of genus and boundary in the finite abelian covering theory of a curve. This fits the classical theory of generalized Jacobians, which incorporates boundary conditions into divisor classes; Milne's Sections 8–9 explain how that broader geometry relates to covers of punctured curves.
history: The classical theory of generalized Jacobians incorporates boundary conditions into the geometry of divisor classes. Milne's Sections 8–9 place punctured-curve covering questions in this broader setting. The formula here expresses the boundary contribution through étale cohomology.

entries.title: Abel–Jacobi identifies the abelianized fundamental group with the full Tate module
entries.summary: Under explicit Picard representation and class-compatibility hypotheses, Abel–Jacobi identifies the abelianized fundamental group with the full Tate module.
statement: Let $C/K$ be a geometrically integral smooth proper curve model over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$, with base point $P$. Supply a smooth proper geometrically connected object $J$ representing the designated degree-zero relative Picard functor, and a morphism $a:C\to J$ whose Poincaré pullbacks give the classes $\mathcal O(Q-P)$ after field extensions.
For every geometric point $\xi$ of $C$, the theorem constructs a continuous group isomorphism
$$e:\pi_1^{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C,\xi)^{\mathrm{ab}}\xrightarrow{\sim}T(J),$$
where $T(J)=\varprojlim_n J(K)[n]$ is the full Tate module. It also proves that $e$ agrees with the map induced by $a$ followed by the fundamental-group/Tate comparison for $J$.
discussion: The compatibility with Abel–Jacobi identifies the geometric morphism that carries abelian covering data into compatible systems of torsion points. It gives a link between covering theory and the Jacobian's torsion beyond an abstract group isomorphism. Milne's Abelian Varieties, Section 15, describes the fundamental-group/Tate-module comparison for abelian varieties, which combines here with the Jacobian's description of abelian covers of a curve.
history: Milne's Abelian Varieties, Section 15, relates the étale fundamental group of an abelian variety to its full Tate module. Together with the Jacobian's description of abelian covers of a curve, this explains the classical bridge between Abel–Jacobi maps, covering theory, and compatible systems of torsion points.

entries.title: Nondegeneracy of the divisorial Weil pairing
entries.summary: Every nonzero torsion divisor class is detected by a character obtained from supplied divisorial Weil-pairing data.
statement: Let $K$ be algebraically closed of characteristic $0$, and let $F/K$ have principal-divisor data. Assume there is a transcendental $t\in F$ with $[F:K(t)]<\infty$. For $n\ge1$, let $w$ be divisorial Weil-pairing data on $\operatorname{Pic}^0(F/K)[n]$: its pairing agrees with divisor evaluation, and torsion classes admit rational divisor representatives avoiding any given finite set of places. Then
$$x\longmapsto\bigl(y\longmapsto w(x,y)\bigr)$$
is injective. In particular, $w(x,y)=1$ for every $y$ implies $x=0$.
discussion: Nondegeneracy allows torsion divisor classes to be studied through their pairing characters. It is what makes the pairing useful for duality and for constraining automorphisms or Galois actions on torsion. The result belongs to classical abelian-variety duality: Milne's Abelian Varieties, Section 16, describes pairings through divisors and rational functions and relates them to torsion in an abelian variety and its dual.
history: The Weil pairing belongs to the classical duality theory of abelian varieties. Milne's Abelian Varieties, Section 16, develops pairings from divisor evaluation and relates them to torsion and dual abelian varieties. The divisorial formulation makes the connection with rational functions and reciprocity explicit.
